surveys have undergone, especially in conducting the socio-economic surveys. Further details
of the changing survey design can be obtained from Lahiri (1954), Sankaranarayanan (2003),
Murthy and Roy (1975) and Manna (2025) among others. All these reflect the degree of
flexibility built into the infrastructural arrangement and the basic framework of t he survey
design. The inbuilt flexibility allows for choice of subjects of enquiry, construction of sampling
frames, finetuning of sampling procedures, and collection of data in the field, depending upon
the users’ needs, availability of required informati on and the field conditions. Lahiri, one of
the associates of Mahalanobis right from the beginning, could foresee the prospects and
commented that “the NSS chose a multi-purpose and multi-subject framework, and the survey
design was gradually so evolved as to permit the study of the inter -connections between the

52
various components of the socio economic picture of the country and its constituent regions
and states.”

During the course of its evolution, the NSSO has confronted useful criticisms that have led to
debates on various methodological issues relating to quality of response. Some of the specific
issues that have come up time and again in deliberations of the scholars and survey practitioners
are the duration of reference period and recall error, leng th of schedules and respondents’
fatigue and respondents’ bias. In the First Round, Mahalanobis and Sen (1954) present a
detailed discussion on the reference period and question its desirability. They mention that
scrutiny from the angle of investigator co nsistency was not considered in the first round, but
interpenetrating sub samples were used from the second round onwards. The question of
reference period cropped up time and again in the future rounds as well (Bhattacharya (2002)).

It is the vision, ten acity and experience of Mahalanobis that put India not far from the centre
of sample surveys map of the world. Discussing the future programme of NSS, the Report on
the First Round notes: “ It is hoped, the National Sample Survey would supply in future a
continuing stream of essential information relating to the economic progress of the country for
purposes of planning and policy discussions.” No wonder, NSS is now a 75-year-old successful
phenomenon, celebrating its Platinum Jubilee.

Glimpses of the 75th Year Celebration of the National Sample Survey (NSS) - From a

The National Sample Survey (NSS) stands as one of the strongest pillars of India’s statistical
excellence since its establishment in 1950 under the visionary leadership of Professor P.C.
Mahalanobis, the father of Indian statistics. Initially focused on rural areas to support national
accounts, the NSS gradually expanded its scope to cover diverse socio -economic dimensions
and both rural and urban populations. Its noble objective has always been to provide reliable,
timely, and comprehensive data to guide India’s socio-economic planning.
Over the past seven and a half decades, the NSS has evolved from a modest sample -based
survey initiative to one of the largest continuous households as well as enterprise survey system
in the world, covering every corner of the country — from metropolitan cities to the remotest
villages. Enterprise surveys have provided crucial insights into the structure, growth, and
financial health of India’s industrial and unincorporated sectors, while the socio -economic
surveys have played a vital role in shaping public policy on key aspects such as employment
& unemployment, consumption on health and education, Debt & Investment, tourism,
migration, disability, time use etc.
The 75th Year Celebration of the NSS symbolized not merely a mi lestone but also a tribute to
India’s data warriors who have worked tirelessly to uphold the values of truthful data,
transparency, and public trust. As India strives toward Viksit Bharat 2047, the Ministry remains
committed to further strengthening these surveys, ensuring that they capture emerging trends
and contribute meaningfully to the formulation of policies that support the sustainable
development of the nation.

Abstract
Empirically, education and skill development have a clear and positive impact on enhancing
productivity, employability, and human capital formation, which contributes significantly to
reducing poverty and destitution. Target 4.4 of Sustainable Development Goal (SDG)-4 seeks
to substantially increase, by 2030, the number of youths and adults who possess relevant job -
oriented skills, including technical and vocational skills, for employment, decent work, and
entrepreneurship.
The present study aims to assess the prevalenc e of ICT skills among individuals in Uttar
Pradesh and at the national level in India. For this purpose, the analysis utilizes ICT skill
variables derived from unit-level data of the 78th Round of the Multiple Indicator Survey (MIS),
conducted in 2020 –21 by the National Statistical Office (NSO), Ministry of Statistics and
Programme Implementation (MoSPI), Government of India. ICT skills are measured through
nine computer-related activity i ndicators, aligned with the framework recommended by the
United Nations.
To evaluate inequality in ICT skill acquisition, the study employs Thiel and Atkinson indices,
the Human Opportunity Index (HOI), and Shapley decomposition methods. The findings reveal
that over 50 percent of youths in Uttar Pradesh lack any form of ICT skills. Shapley
decomposition highlights that education is the most significant contributor to inequality in ICT
skill attainment, followed closely by the area of residence.
The analysis underscores the urgent need for comprehensive policy interventions to integrate

The Theil Index is grounded in the principles of information theory and conceptualizes income
inequality as a form of entropy or disorder in the distribution of income across individuals. It
measures the divergence of actual income shares from a perfectly equal distribution, without
embedding normative j udgments. As a statistical measure, the Theil Index is particularly 7

valued for its property of decomposability, which allows overall inequality to be broken down
into within-group and between-group components. This feature makes it especially useful in
analyzing inequality across subpopulations, regions, or sectors. In contrast, the Atkinson Index
originates from welfare economics and incorporates explicit value judgments regarding the
social desirability of different income distributions. It employs an ine quality aversion
parameter (ε), which captures the degree to which a society is concerned about income
disparities. A higher value of ε indicates a stronger preference for equality, thereby allowing
the Atkinson Index to reflect ethical perspectives on inc ome distribution. As such, while the
Theil Index serves as a descriptive tool, the Atkinson Index functions as a normative measure
that links inequality directly to social welfare considerations.
The sensitivity of the Theil and Atkinson indices differs n otably in terms of the segments of
the income distribution they emphasize. The Theil Index tends to be more responsive to
variations at the upper end of the income spectrum, thereby highlighting inequalities driven by
high-income individuals earning disproportionately more than the average. This makes it well-
suited for identifying top -heavy inequality and for contexts where rising incomes among the
wealthy are a primary concern. The Atkinson Index, by contrast, allows for flexibility in
sensitivity through its inequality aversion parameter. When ε is set to a higher value, the index
becomes more sensitive to changes in the lower tail of the income distribution, effectively
placing greater weight on income losses among the poor. This sensitivity to lower -income
groups makes the Atkinson Index particularly appropriate for

placing greater weight on income losses among the poor. This sensitivity to lower -income
groups makes the Atkinson Index particularly appropriate for evaluating redistributive policies
and poverty alleviation efforts, as it aligns more closely with concerns about economic justice
and social equity.

basic opportunities. Higher the value of HOI better distribution of resources.

Discussion
The future of work will mainly be a technology driven era especially ICT based work .Any
kind of future job will involve use of technology as a part of the work. Therefore, the
knowledge of ICT will be the basic requirement and the potential job seekers cannot ignore
this fact. The present paper attempted to analyse level of ICT skill among the all ages and
youths at the country level as well as for the state of Uttar Pradesh. It also attempted to measure
the inequality in ICT skills and their potential sources. The findings present a poor picture of
ICT literacy among the individuals across the country in general and in the state in particular.
For all ages, number of people with no ICT skills is very high. However, the main cause of

Rabinarayan Patra2 Abstract Financial inclusion (FI) has been a vital strategy for fostering inclusive economic growth in
India. With a vast population of diverse socio -economic-demographic backgrounds and
significant rural presence, ensuring access to and usage of affordable and appropriate financial
services to the people and businesses has been a major challenge both at the national and sub-
national levels. Recognizing this, the government, along with the Reserve Bank of India (RBI)
and various financial institutions, has implemented a range of initiatives—such as the Pradhan
Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (PMJDY), digital banking, and mobile p ayment systems — and
innovative models — such as the Business Correspondent model — to bring the unbanked and
underbanked into the formal financial system. India’s strategy has been dynamic, evolved and
developed with experience and changing national and gl obal environment. This paper is an
attempt to ascertain the current status of FI across the country and sub-groups of population by
using the 78th round (2020-21) NSS data. The study finds statistically significant variations in
the extent of FI across soc io-economic-demographic groups of population. While more than
87 per cent of the national adult population is financially included, the progress ranges from
95.9 per cent in Karnataka to 65.5 per cent in Meghalaya. Concerted demand side interventions
are necessary to correct the situation.

The present study builds upon extensive existing literature and identification of gaps in research

. Review of literature: insights and gaps
The present study builds upon extensive existing literature and identification of gaps in research
conducted so far. With a preliminary discussion on the theoretical underpinnings and the
benefits of financial inclusion, it proceeds in four sub -sections: firstly, to find out whether FI
is voluntary or policy induced, i.e., to take advantage of benefits from government policy;
secondly, to understand the factors determining FI; thirdly, to explain disparities and fourthly,
to identify gaps in previous research.
The Evolutionary Theory of Economic Change and innovation (Schumpeter, 1911, 1939),
behavioural theory (Nelson and Win ter, 1982), theory of accessing opportunities (Beck &
Torre, 2006), public goods theory of financial inclusion (Ozili, 2020), financial liberalization
theory (McKinnon, 1973; Shaw, 1973), Access barrier theory ( Honohan, 2004; Chamberlain

behavioural theory (Nelson and Win ter, 1982), theory of accessing opportunities (Beck &
Torre, 2006), public goods theory of financial inclusion (Ozili, 2020), financial liberalization
theory (McKinnon, 1973; Shaw, 1973), Access barrier theory ( Honohan, 2004; Chamberlain
& Walter, 2005), social capital theory (Granovetter, 1973), and the theory of information
asymmetry (Akerlof, 1980) may be the fundamental theories backing the empirics of financial
inclusion, a lack of it or exclusion.
Accessing financial institutions and using financial services offers three major benefits, viz.
safe holding of money, meeting consumption needs in hard times, and harnessing investment
opportunities (Deaton, 1990; Dupas & Robinson, 2013) while using agricultural finance can
significantly increase farmers’ incomes contributing to the growth of the agricultural gross
domestic product (GDP) (World Bank, 2008). It encourages innovation and technology
adoption, and enables taking risks (Schumpeter, 1934). FI positively correlates with GDP 28

growth and poverty redu ction in Bangladesh (Hasan et al., 2024) and additionally having a
significant impact on reducing income inequality in 116 developing countries (Omar and Inaba,
2020). From their study of 22 Sub -Sahara African (SSA) countries for 2012 – 2018, Ifediora
et al. (2022) found that financial inclusion has a positive impact on economic growth. FI leads
to increase in gross domestic product and total factor productivity (Dabla -Norris et al., 2015).
A broader outreach of finance enables talented newcomers from disad vantaged groups to be
empowered (Beck & de la Torre, 2006). FI helps in achieving 7 of the 17 Sustainable
Development Goals (SDGs), ending poverty, boosting entrepreneurship, increasing
employment, promoting economic growth and supporting women's economic empowerment
(World Bank, 2025). It allows women to have greater control over their financial lives, and can
help themselves and their families to come out of poverty, reduce their risk of falling into
poverty, eliminate their exploitation from the informal sector and increase their ability to fully
engage in productive economic activities (Wadhwa 2022). It also enhances financial well-being
(Herrerias and Alvarez, (n.d.)).
3.1 Policy Induced or Voluntary Participation
In India, the broad objective of FI has been to make financial institutions, products and services
accessible to individuals and businesses and it dates back to the 1900s. Establishment of credit
co-operatives in 1904, bank nationalization in 1969 and 1980, financial liberalisation since
1991 a nd financial inclusion as an explicit policy in 2005 pursued both intensively and
extensively thereafter marked the four phases of FI which may be christened as activist,
expansionist, promotional and modernist milestones of FI Policy

were the mainstay in the initial phase, banks including regional rural banks with focus on mass
banking acted as harbingers in the second phase, liberalisation played the role of accelerator in
the third phase and reaching the last mile in financ ial development is at the very heart of FI
since 2005.

3.2 Determinants of FI
The purpose of this paper is to investigate the relationship between the financial inclusion and
development variables in India. It is, therefore, essential to understand the actual level of
inclusion and its determinants to improve FI in the nation. Research has shown that micro-level
factors such as age, gender, educational qualification, and income level are vital determinants
of financial inclusion (Zhang and Posso, 2019; Koomson and Danquah, 2021). Lee et al. (2022)
emphasized that countries with low risk-related uncertainties and terrorism threats experience
higher financial inclusion. Soumare et al. (2016) highlighted the importance of trustworthy
financial institutions for a financially inclusive financial sector. In the context of emerging Sub-
Saharan African economies, Asuming et al. (2019) pointed out that promot ing favourable
business conditions can enhance financial inclusion in Sub -Saharan African emerging
economies.

and north-eastern states outperform others in terms of financial inclusion, with urban, richer,
educated, and salaried individuals having higher chances of financial inclusion. Chu's (2019)
study on financial inclusion across 144 countries using the 2017 Global Findex database, found

3.4 Research Gaps Despite growing attention to financial inclusion, significant gaps remain in existing research.
Much of the current literature focuses on access to formal financial services, often overlooking
usage quality, informal systems, and long -term impact. There is also limited research on
marginalized populations, such as rural communities, women, and minority social groups.
Additionally, regional studies are unevenly distributed, with a concentration in urban and high-
income settings. Addressing these gaps is crucial for developing more equitable and effective
financial inclusion strategies. Here are some key gaps in research on financial inclusion:

Financial inclusion is an important condition for inclusive development and an enabler for
several SDGs. India has achieved a remarkable feat in FI, where more than four -fifth of the
adult population were having access to bank accounts. Though marginal variation is observed
in FI between EAG and Non -EAG states, but the performance in some of the north -eastern
states are far below the national average. Middle aged and elderly population have an edge
over younger age population in FI and higher education and employability impact it favourably.
FI among household heads was much better compared to the other members of the household.
Population from lower socio -economic strata is less likely to have FI in spite of various
enthusiastic policies in place. Muslims and other minority communities, larger family size
households, living in urban areas, and never married ar e less likely to have FI. Even though
Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (PMJDY) was successful in bringing 29.56 crore women
within the purview of FI (Economic Times, 2024), but they continue to fall behind men by a
considerable margin. “The Jan Dhan Yojana has garnered global praise for its transformative
impact on FI in India and in 2023, a G20 report by the World Bank reveals that India has 40

achieved its FI goals in just 6 years, a feat that would have taken 47 years without its advanced
Digital Public Infra structure” (Economic Times, 2024) . The Global Findex which is the
world’s most comprehensive database on financial inclusion shows that in India the number of
adults (age 15+) with an account reached to 77.5 percent in 2021 from 35.2 percent in 2011
and 54 .3 percent adults opened first account to receive a wage or government payment.
Similarly, 77.6 percent adult women, 78.3 percent adults in the poorest 40 percent households
and 67.5 percent youth (age 15 -24) were having accounts. In other dimensions of FI , 34.9
percent adults, 28 percent women and 26 percent adults in the poorest 40 percent households
had made or received digital payment in the past year. About 34.5 percent adults used accounts
to store money for cash management and 44.8 percent adults had borrowed any money in the
past year (Demirgüç-Kunt et al., 2022). RBI’s multidimensional composite FI Index also shows
continuous improvement in FI as the composite score increased from 43.4 in 2017 to 64.2 in
2024. So, there is no doubt that the level of financial inclusion in our country has improved a
lot over the last few years but still some states and sub-groups of population are lagging behind.
Therefore, to achieve universal financial inclusion focus should be given to those states and
regions and sub-groups of population where the levels of financial inclusion are low, and on
the usage and quality aspects so that it can act as a vibrant enable r for several sustainable
development goals.

Assessing the Productivity-Investment Nexus in Informal Economy: Evidence from India
Sonakhya Samaddar1
Ujjaval Srivastava2
Abstract
Capital investment is deemed as one of the key factors in boosting the growth of a business.
This study attempts to examine the relationship between productivity and capital investments
in various sectors of the informal economy, utili zing unit-level data from the Annual Survey
of Unincorporated Sector Enterprises (ASUSE) 2023 -24. The primary objective is to assess
how capital investment influence productivity in informal firms, with particular attention to
sectoral and operational distinctions. The analysis also incorporates auxiliary variables such as
the adoption of information and communication technology (ICT) and access to financial
assistance. The findings reveal a statistically significant association between capital investment
and productivity across all three major sectors—manufacturing, trade, and services. However,
the magnitude of the effect is notably higher for self -run establishments in the manufacturing
sector, while the relationship is weak for establishments employing h ired workers. Moreover,
the study uncovers that ICT adoption and financial assistance significantly enhance
productivity, particularly among self -operated businesses in the manufacturing and services
sectors. Conversely, for establishments with hired labou r, investment in human capital —
through emoluments and wages —emerges as the primary driver of productivity gains. These
findings contribute to our understanding of the complex dynamics between capital investment,
productivity, and labour across different sectors and establishment types, offering implications
for resource allocation and policy considerations.

Informality has no universally accepted single definition; it is generally conceived as
something which maintains no legal records or cannot be found in any legal framework. The
National Statistics Office (NSO) of India, measures absorption of workforce in the informal

significant amount of labour from varied background. It is a space where the accumulation of

3. Data Description and Methodological Approach
Data Description:
The empirical analysis is based on unit-level data from the Annual Survey of Unincorporated
Sector Enterprises (ASUSE) for the period 2023 –24. ASUSE provides comprehensive
information on operational and financial characteristics of unorganized enterprises in India,
categorized into Own Account Enterprises (OAE) and establishments with Hired Workers
(HWE). It covers those businesses which are not registered under Companies Act and thus
includes in its coverage some establishments which are registered with other authorities (like
ESIC, GSTN etc.) and also a very small proportion of establishments maintaining audited
books of accounts. However, around 99% of the business covered in this survey are proprietary
and partnership establishments which are mostly unregul ated and self -employed, thus,
emphasizing that it is great source of information for the assumed informal sector.
This study specifically utilizes data from ASUSE 2023–24, which was conducted during the
period October 2023 to September 2024, covering 4,98,024 establishments across rural and
urban regions and encompassing three broad industrial categories: manufacturing, trade, and
other services. Given the unorganized and informal nature of the sector, approximately 99%
of the sampled establishments provided oral estimates based on the reference period of the
last 30 days , while the remaining enterprises, typically larger or more formalized units,
reported audited annual financial data.

5. Discussion
The findings of this study provide a robust empirical basis for understanding productivity
determinants within India's unincorporated sector, revealing both universal drivers and sector-
specific nuances. The results are largely consistent with established economic literature and
offer critical insights for policy formulation.
A central and compe lling finding is the unequivocal importance of capital investment as key
engines of productivity. Our result that a higher capital-labour ratio (as measured by the log of
assets per worker) is a primary driver of output is a fundamental tenet of economic t heory,
aligning with the Solow -Swan model (Solow, 1956) and other neoclassical growth
frameworks. This capital accumulation process is intrinsically linked to the significant positive
effect of loan availability. Our findings show that enterprises with acc ess to loans have
significantly higher productivity, confirming that financial services are a key channel through
which unincorporated businesses can acquire the necessary capital for investment and
expansion. This also empirically supports concerns raised by the World Bank regarding the
need for finance to enable an inclusive economic recovery (World Bank, 2020).
The roles of human capital and technology adoption also emerge as significant factors, albeit
with some sector-specific variations. For establishments with hired workers, the strong positive
correlation between the emoluments per worker and productivity supports both Human Capital
Theory (Becker, 1964) and efficiency wage theory (Stiglitz, 1987). Higher compensation likely
attracts and retains more skilled labour, while also increasing worker

attracts and retains more skilled labour, while also increasing worker motivation and effort.
The adoption of ICT consistently shows a positive and significant impact on output per worker,
particularly in own -account establishments. This finding aligns with literature that confirm s
the sustained positive impact of digital technologies on enterprise performance, even in
informal and resource-constrained environments. Notably, Gupta and Kumar (2018) leveraged
data from the National Statistics Office to reveal that even small -scale en terprises—often
limited in technological reach —experience notable gains in both firm -level and labor
productivity through ICT integration. Further, Aterido et al. (2018) provide cross -country
evidence that ICT use significantly boosts productivity and employment outcomes, especially
for small and medium enterprises operating in developing economies. Their findings reinforce
the argument that digital inclusion is a key lever for economic empowerment and
competitiveness in informal sectors.
The analysis of lo cation-specific variables highlights the heterogeneous landscape of the
unincorporated sector. The consistently positive and significant coefficients for an urban
location provide strong empirical support for agglomeration economies, a concept central to
the field of New Economic Geography (Krugman, 1991). Urban areas provide clear
productivity advantages through better infrastructure, larger markets, and access to a denser
network of labour and knowledge (Glaeser & Resseger, 2010). The urban advantage amplifies 59

the impact of ICT adoption, creating an ecosystem where technology -driven growth is more
feasible and sustainable. (World Bank, 2017).
While many of our findings are consistent with established economic theory, several results
are particularly nuance d and even contrast with common expectations in the literature. The
most striking of these is the relationship between the age of establishment and productivity.
For most sectors, older establishments are more productive, a finding consistent with the
concept of "learning-by-doing". However, for hired worker service establishments, being older
is associated with a negative and significant coefficient. This finding challenges the
conventional view of accumulated experience as a universal source of productivi ty gains.
Instead, it suggests a process of creative destruction, where newer, more agile firms are better
equipped to adapt to new technologies and business models, thus outperforming older, less
flexible competitors (Schumpeter, 1942). This is further su pported by recent studies on firm
dynamics that link innovation to growth and highlight that older firms may struggle to innovate
(Coad et al., 2016). In line with this, Huergo and Jaumandreu (2004) demonstrate that the
probability of innovation tends to decline as firms age—young and mid-life firms show higher
innovation activity, while older firms, often constrained by organizational inertia and risk
aversion, innovate less. This decline in innovation capacity reinforces the notion that age may
hinder not just adaptability, but also the pursuit of productivity-enhancing advancements.
A notable exception to general findings is the positive and significant effect of household
location on hired worker trading establishments. This result contrasts with much of the

l findings is the positive and significant effect of household
location on hired worker trading establishments. This result contrasts with much of the existing
literature, which identifies home-based operations as a growth constraint due to limited space
and inadequate commercial infrastructure (Henderson, 2002). Yet, findings from Muthusamy
and Ibrahim (2016) reveal that home -based workers in India 's informal sector remain among
the most vulnerable—receiving low wages under piece-rate systems, lacking legal protection,
and possessing limited bargaining power. Despite these disadvantages, the present result
suggests that for certain trading activitie s, a home -based business model may confer
competitive advantages through reduced overhead costs and streamlined, family -based
supervision of hired labour. Such a paradox underscores the need for a more granular, sector -
specific understanding of informal economy dynamics.
While this study provides important insights, several limitations should be noted. The cross -
sectional nature of the data limits our ability to make causal inferences. Additionally, it would
be interesting to perform a detailed analysis for different industries under each broad sectors of
the economy. Future research using longitudinal data could provide additional insights into the
dynamics of productivity determination.
6. Conclusion
This study highlights the pivotal role of fixed capital and human capital in driving productivity
among unincorporated small enterprises, with particularly strong effects observed in the
manufacturing sector—a cornerstone of India’s journey toward Viksit Bharat. The empirical
evidence underscores the need for targeted policy interventions and improved financial

60

accessibility to support business investment. These mechanisms are essential for strengthening
the informal economy, enabling structural transformation, and enhancing productivity within
a traditionally underperforming segment. In doing so, they contribute meaningfully to broader
developmental goals and sustainable economic growth.
The findings offer a nuanced understanding of the productivity dynamics wit hin India’s
unincorporated sector. They emphasize the importance of multifaceted policy approaches,
especially those that expand access to formal finance, encourage capital investment, foster ICT
adoption and digital literacy, and promote regionally balanc ed development to bridge the
urban–rural divide.
Furthermore, the study reveals significant variations in productivity outcomes based on
establishment age and household location, illustrating the limitations of uniform policy
frameworks. Instead, the evidence advocates for tailored, sector-specific strategies that reflect
the diverse realities of informal enterprises —maximizing their productivity potential and
aligning with inclusive growth objectives. 61

Abstract
This paper analyses access to drinking water and sanitation services in India using National
Sample Survey (NSS) data for the years 2012, 2018, and 2020 –21. It considers Water,
Sanitation, and Hygiene (WASH) services not only in terms of basic infrastructu re coverage
but also for ensuring service quality, safety, and equity. The study reveals that while basic
access to water and sanitation has expanded significantly, stark inequalities persist in higher -
level services that can guarantee reliability and hygi enic standards. These disparities are
especially pronounced across caste, religious, and expenditure groups, with Scheduled Castes
(SCs), Scheduled Tribes (STs) and Muslims remaining disadvantaged, particularly in accessing
piped water within premises and exclusive hygienic latrines. State -level correlation analysis
reveals that higher -level services are positively associated with state -level development
indicators of urbanization and household expenditure and negatively with poverty whereas
basic coverage shows minimal impact of these structural factors.
These findings highlight the need to shift focus from headlines of universal coverage towards
ensuring service quality, safety, and equitable outcomes. Targeted interventions for lagging
social groups and states, coupled with investments in functional infrastructure, faecal sludge
management and behavior change, are critical to bridging the persistent “hygiene gap.” By
adopting a disaggregated and service -quality–oriented approach to WASH, this paper

1. Introduction
Access to safe drinking water and adequate sanitation is not merely a fundamental human right
but a key determinant of public health, dignity, and socioeconomic well -being. Over the past
couple of decades, India has witnessed an unprecedented push to ensur e universal access to
safe drinking water and sanitation by launching flagship missions such as the Swachh Bharat
Mission (SBM), Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban Transformation (AMRUT) and the
Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) (MoHUA, 2021; Ministry of Jal S hakti, 2021). Together, these set
ambitious targets of achieving piped‑water coverage of every rural and urban household,
eliminating open defecation, and upgrading urban sanitation systems. These efforts are closely
aligned with Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 6, which seeks to ensure universal access
to water and sanitation. These are evaluated against the WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring
Programme (JMP) service ladders that emphasize the progression from basic access to safely
managed services (United Nations, 2015). The JMP framework clarifies that real progress lies
not only in infrastructure coverage but also in ensuring service quality, safety, and equity
(WHO/UNICEF, 2017).
Despite considerable policy attention and financial investment, disparities in access to these
basic services remain deeply embedded along the axes of caste, religion, economic status and
levels of regional development. This paper examines the access to drinking water and sanitation
facilities across various social and religious groups, economic strata, and states in India, using
two-tiered classification of ‘lower-level’ and ‘higher-level’ services. This approach allows us
to capture both the apparent convergence in basic coverage along with the persistent
inequalities in

‘higher-level’ services. This approach allows us
to capture both the apparent convergence in basic coverage along with the persistent
inequalities in reliable, hygienic services and explore how these disparities manifest across the
development spectrum.
The study is guided by two central questions. First, how equitably are drinking water and
sanitation facilities distributed across Scheduled Castes (SC), Scheduled Tribes (ST), Other
Castes, and religious groups including Hindus, Muslims, Christians and Others? Second, to
what extent do disparities in access to water and sanitation services—particularly higher-level,
reliable services—correlate with household expend iture and macro -level state development
indicators of urbanization, poverty, and development? We hypothesize that while India has
approached near-universal coverage in basic access over time, significant inequalities persist
in the provision of secure, rel iable, and hygienic services —gaps that are strongly associated
with social identity, affordability, and spatial development. The conceptual distinction between
‘lower-level’ and ‘higher -level’ facilities forms a crucial axis of analysis, enabling an
investigation into the hypothesis that although there is convergence in the access over time
across socio-economic groups and states for the basic facilities, the inequality in the availability
of secure and reliable services meeting the norms of safety, convenience, and modernity, elude
large segments of households. These deficits can indeed be explained in terms caste, religion,
affordability and spatial development parameters.

gaps in functionality, quality, and inclusivity. By focusing on the quality and equity in WASH

investments bridge the ‘hygiene gap,’ particularly for marginalized groups and lagging regions.

2.2 Categorization of Service Levels
Over time, global frameworks for monitoring access to water and sanitation have shifted
focus—from basic coverage under the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) to quality,
safety, and equity under the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). The MDG-era target (7C)
emphasized access to "improved" sources of drinking water and sanitation, as defined by the
WHO–UNICEF JMP. However, these classifications faced criticism for overlooking service
quality. Research revealed that “improved” sources often remained contaminated (Bain et al.,
2012; Jalan & Somanathan, 2008), and many sanitation facilities were unhygienic or shared,
limiting health impact and user dignity. Responding to these concerns, SDG 6 calls for
universal and equitable access to safe and affordable drinking water and adequate and inclusive
sanitation and hygiene for all by 2030. To reflect this global shift, the current study adopts a
two-tiered classification framework, aligned with the updated JMP ladder (2017), as discussed
above.

2.3 Development Indicators and Correlation Analysis
To understand the broader context in which households gain access to drinking water and
sanitation services, the study attempts to explore the association between key WASH indicators
and selected macro-level development characteristics across Indian states. Three indicators are
considered: (i) the level of urbanization (percentage of households residing in urban areas), (ii)
Monthly Per Capita Consumption Expenditure (MPCE) a s a proxy for average household
economic status, and (iii) the poverty rate, measured as the proportion of the population living
below the poverty line. These indicators provide a macro -level backdrop to assess how
demographic and economic differences may be associated with access to different tiers of
WASH services.
Pearson correlation coefficients are computed for the years 2012, 2018, and 2020 –21 to
examine these associations across time. This approach allows us to observe whether states with
higher average consumption or greater urban population consistently report improved access
to drinking water and sanitation, especially for higher -order services. Similarly, negative
associations with poverty levels help to understand the degree to which deprivation limits
access to safe and reliable WASH services. This multi -year correlation analysis, thus,
complements the descriptive assessment by providing a clearer picture of the structural
variation across states.

3. Access to Drinking Water and Sanitation facilities of different levels: Emerging pattern
and interdependencies with Development Indicators at State Level (2012–2021)
India has launched major Flagship programmes—beginning with the National Rural Drinking
Water Programme (NRDWP), now re‑envisioned as the Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM), and the
Swachh Bharat Mission (SBM) in both its rural and urban streams — invested heavily in
infrastructure, behaviour‑change campaigns, and institutional reforms, declared itself Open
Defecation Free (ODF) in 2019, marking a symbolic milestone while JJM aims at universal
rural tap water access by 2024. However, a critical question remains: has this expansion
translated into equitable and sustainable services across all states? Beneath these headline 80

narratives of success lie deeper spatial, social, and economic gradients in both access and
quality of WASH services. Infrastructure alone cannot guarantee convenient and reliable water
supply, privacy and hygiene in sanitation facilities, or safe management of excreta. Moreover,
aggregate national figures often mask entrenched inequities —between richer and poorer
households, between rapidly urbanizing and predominantly rural states, and between well‑off
urban wards and informal settlements.
To unpack these patterns, the present section examines how access to different levels of
drinking water and sanitation facilities has evolved over the past decade and how this access is
intertwined with broader development indicators —level of urbanisation, monthly household
consumption expenditure (as a proxy for affluence), and poverty rate across Indian states. An
attempt is made here to develop this understanding through the interpretation of the correlations
in the following sections.
3.1 Drinking Water: From Uniform Coverage to Differentiated Service Quality
Although overall access to ‘lower-level’ of drinking‐water sources expanded rapidly betwe en
2012 and 2021, the correlations confirm that this has been remarkably uniform across states—
showing no significant association with levels of urbanisation, household expenditure, or
poverty at any of the three time points. For example, both Gujarat and Odisha reported
comparable levels of improved source coverage despite differences in development status,
reflecting the impact of the universal nature of infrastructure-driven efforts like the Jal Jeevan
Mission.
However, once we shift focus from mere cove rage to better service quality —measured as
improved sources located within premises and receiving adequate water year‐round

hift focus from mere cove rage to better service quality —measured as
improved sources located within premises and receiving adequate water year‐round —a
different picture emerges. In both 2018 and 2021, these service‐quality indicators exhibit
statistically significant correlations with structural factors. More urbanised states like Kerala
and Tamil Nadu saw substantially higher proportions of households enjoying in‐premises,
reliable supply, manifested in a positive correlation in later rounds. Wealthier states such as
Punjab and Ma harashtra demonstrated stronger in‐home service quality, reinforcing a
significant positive alignment with affordability by 2018, persisting in 2021. Conversely,
higher-poverty states—exemplified by Bihar and Uttar Pradesh —lagged markedly in reliable
in-premises service, underpinning a significant negative association.
That these associations are insignificant in 2012 but become significant in 2018 and 2021
reflects the limitations of drawing inference from blanket coverage metrics. Early in the decade,
intensified infrastructure investment under national programmes succeeded in widening basic
access almost uniformly, obscuring deeper inequities. As systems matured, the ability to deliver
water within the household and throughout the year became increasingly dependent on state
capacity, urban management, and household wealth —hence the emergence of significant
correlations in the latter two survey rounds.
This pattern indicates a critical policy lesson: “Improved source” coverage alone is an
insufficient proxy for water service equity. To close persistent quality and reliability gaps,
future interventions must target the institutional and financial determinants of the quality -of-
service delivery in lagging states—rather than relying

ture interventions must target the institutional and financial determinants of the quality -of-
service delivery in lagging states—rather than relying solely on expanding nominal coverage. 81

3.2 Sanitation Equity: From Coverage to Quality and the Hygiene Gap
In contrast to water source indicators, access to sanitation —defined as the presence of any
latrine facility (private or shared) —reveals robust and enduring correlations with str uctural
development indicators (Table 7). In 2012, the correlation between access to basic facilities
latrines and household expenditure was already strong (+0.520 in rural areas and +0.533 in
urban areas), while poverty was negatively correlated with latrine access (–0.431 rural, –0.565
urban). By 2021, these relationships got strengthened, with richer and more urban states
continuing to outperform their poorer, less urbanized counterparts. This stratification is not
surprising when we examine state-wise implementation of SBM. States like Maharashtra and
Gujarat had pre-existing sanitation programs and institutional mechanisms, allowing them to
rapidly scale up their toilet construction. In urban Maharashtra, integration with municipal
finance and decentral ized delivery under Urban Local Bodies ensured widespread and
relatively sustained adoption of individual household latrines (IHHLs). In contrast, states such
as Odisha, Jharkhand, and Chhattisgarh, despite receiving substantial SBM grants, struggled
with supply-side constraints, weak rural outreach, and limited local governance capacity. These
states show consistently lower sanitation coverage, particularly in rural areas. More
importantly, the correlation data reveal that even the basic latrine access is far from universal,
and the structural inequities observed were not been fully addressed in 2012. More importantly,
despite over 100 million toilets reportedly constructed under SBM between 2014 and 2020,
poorer states and low-income households continue to lag in

despite over 100 million toilets reportedly constructed under SBM between 2014 and 2020,
poorer states and low-income households continue to lag in access, reflecting the inability of

Sanitation quality indicators—such as whether latrines are private (non -shared), covered, and
hygienic (with safe excreta disposal)—expose a deeper layer of inequality. Here, correlations
with expenditure and urbanization are not only higher than for basic access but have also
intensified over time. In 2012, private latrines correlated at +0.507 with household expenditure

indicators make it clear that merely constructing latrines does not guarantee safety, dignity, or
public health gains. For instance, many states declared ODF sta tus based on individual

The key findings emerging from the analysis is that the access to lower -level water and
sanitation facilities is relatively widespread and shows weak correlation with household
expenditure levels or other indicators of development at state level. This suggests that basic
provisioning has penetrated across large segments of the population, including lower-income
strata, socially marginalized groups and less developed states. However, when it comes to

The correlation matrices at three points of time reflect a sobering reality of temporal dynamics

the underlying inequalities across the states in water quantity and sanitation quality have not
only persisted but in some cases worsened. The poverty gradient in sanitation access and
quality remains stubbornly high. Urbanization, while generally enabling better WASH
outcomes, has n ot ensured equity. Moreover, the deepening correlations between household
expenditure and WASH quality indicators suggest that public provisioning is insufficient to

India has entered a new phase in its WASH journey. With infrastructure expansion nearing
saturation, attention must turn to deepening quality, convenience, sustainability, and equity.
While official statistics report high le vels of coverage for water and sanitation, such figures 84

often conflate access to any facility —however inadequate or unreliable —with access to
facilities that meet the standards of safety, hygiene, and dignity. essential for improving health
outcomes and qu ality of life. By showing that basic access has become more democratized
while advanced access remains strongly stratified, the study adds a few empirical concerns to
ongoing debates about equity in service delivery and the politics of infrastructure development.
To address these, policy makers must embrace differentiated strategies. High -poverty states
require targeted technical assistance, outcome -based financing, and behavioural nudges
tailored to local contexts. Urban sanitation must move beyond toilet targets to regulated FSSM
ecosystems, especially in slums and peri-urban zones. The hygiene gap must become a central

economic life on equal terms (Ravi, 2022). For marginalized communities and people living in
less developed states, the absence of safe water and sanitation can reinforce existing
vulnerabilities and restrict opportunities for education, employment and mobility. Conversely,
access to higher -level facilities can signal inclusion and recognition by the state, thereby
contributing to the social integration of historically excluded groups. States such as Kerala,

Divisional Paper of HSD1
Abstract:
The National Statistics Office (NSO), Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation
(MoSPI), is responsible for conducting nationwide integrated large scale sample surveys
employing scientific sampling methods to generate data and statistical indicators on diverse
socio-economic aspects through PAPI 2 and CAPI3 mode. Recognising the increasing demand
for alternative modalities of collection of data, a pilot telephonic survey was undertaken in
collaboration with the Population Council Institute (PCI), New Delhi. As the National Statistics
Office (NSO) had not previously conducted any perception-based survey, the telephonic mode
was piloted for the first time to collect data on the perception -based SDG Indicator 16.1.4 —
Proportion of population that feel safe walking alone around the area they live after dark. This
study explores the feasibility of telephonic data collection. The survey was conducted in two
separate geographical locations covering both rural and urban areas. For comparison purposes,
data were obtained using both telephonic and face -to-face interview modes. SDG indicator
16.1.4 is a globally prescribed indicator under the custody of United Nations Office on Drugs
and Crime (UNODC). This study also proposes a revised defin ition of the indicator, with
comparative estimates derived from the collected data.

3. Definition of the SDG indicator 16.1.4 as per UN
United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) is the custodian of this indicator. This
indicator refers to “the proportion of the adult population who feel safe walking alone in their
neighbourhood after dark.”

depending on cultural, physical and language context. Providing a universally applicable
definition of neighbourhood is challenging, as one’s neighbourhood is a subjective concept
that will mean different things to different people. For the purpose of this pilot,
neighbourhood was defined as the vicinity of the respondent’s usual/current residence,
where the respondent usually travels. The definition was quantified in terms of time duration
of walking or distance of walking. Any place within 1-1.5 kilometres from the respondent’s
house or within 15 -20 minutes of walking distance in any direction was considered as

Evolution of Survey Tools and Techniques Used by NSS in Data Collection and Processing
- Divisional Paper of ESD1
Abstract:
The National Sample Survey (NSS), instituted in 1950, has been instrumental to carry out
nationwide large-scale sample surveys in order to provide timely and reliable statistics to aid
evidence-based policy formulation and socio -economic planning. In its early decades, data
collection was entirely manual, involvi ng paper schedules and card -punch-based digitization,
which resulted in considerable delays and potential transcription errors. Over time, NSS
adopted various in-house software solutions at various stages from data collection to processing
and tabulation which gradually helped in improving accuracy and efficiency. The introduction
of e-schedules enabled basic validation checks at the point of data entry, reducing the burden
of post-entry scrutiny and enhancing data integrity.
A major shift occurred with the development of Computer -Assisted Personal Interviewing
(CAPI) and development of web -portal for Annual Surveys of Industries (ASI) and their
integration in e -SIGMA—a comprehensive, server -based platform supporting multi -survey
deployment, real -time valida tion, and automated monitoring. These advancements have
streamlined workflows, minimized delays, and improved overall data quality. This paper
examines the NSS's technological evolution for Annual Surveys of Industries (ASI) and other
household/enterprise surveys, underscoring its proactive adoption of digital tools and its central
role in modernizing India’s official statistics framework.

Introduction:
The National Sample Survey Office (NSSO) was established in 1950 with the aim of creating
a permanent institution dedicated to collecting data on various economic and social aspects of
the country. To support informed socio -economic planning and policy decisions, NSSO
conducts large -scale nationwide surveys under the banner of the National Sample Survey
(NSS). Data collection and processing are crucial stages in any sample survey, as they pave the
way for publishing the survey findings. Over time, with the introduction of advanced
technologies and tools, the National Sample Survey (NSS) has significantly improved its data
collection and processing techniques, leading to a noticeable decrease in the time taken
between planning new surveys and releasing their results.
Historically, NSS relied on Paper Assisted Personal Interview (PAPI) for data collection, where
field investigators visited households and manually recorded r esponses. This information
captured in paper schedule were digitized through data entry module by another group of
officials posted at Data Processing Centres (DPC) located at different places in India. Paper
schedules needed to be dispatched from differen t field offices to DPCs by post and hence a
good amount of time was consumed to even initiate the data digitization job. Ensuring accuracy
in data digitization was also a great challenge which necessitated re -entry of the schedules by
different persons to check transcription error, if any, in the data. After re-entry of the schedule,
the data were subjected to multiple steps of scrutiny to ensure accuracy and credibility. This
prolonged the entire process —from data collection to validation and final release of results.
Similar was the case for Annual Survey of Industries (ASI) which

Similar was the case for Annual Survey of Industries (ASI) which has undergone a remarkable
technological transformation in its methods of data collection and processing since its inception
in 1960. Over time, the adoption of new technologies and tools has significantly streamlined
these procedures. Innovations have helped in reducing manual effort, improve data accuracy,
and most importantly, shorten the time lag between survey execution and release of data.
Data processing in the initial years:
In early years of the National Sample Survey (NSS), up until about four decades ago, data
transcription was performed at Data Processing Centres (DPCs) using the card punching
method. The output of data transcription was collected from a different place in specific storage
device. At that time all software development related to data validation, multiplier generation
and tabulation were entrusted with Computer Centre (CC), New Delhi. Data collected in the
field though Paper Assisted Personal Interview (PAPI) method were digitized at DPCs by card
punching and then sent to CC wherein validation software was run on it to generate error list.
The error list, again, was sent back to Data Processing Division (DPD) for thorough checking
with the actual paper sch edule. Correspondence with FOD was made simultaneously as and
when any anomaly in the data was found. This process had to be performed multiple times to
arrive at a reliable and viable data which were used further for table generation. Generation of
multipliers and tables were also carried out in CC and the output was again shared with DPD
and SDRD for further checking. Correspondence with FOD would generally continue until 109

both data and tables were finalized. Finally, the unit level data were brought out i n public
domain following which multiple reports were prepared for the policy makers and researchers.
With the arrival of D20 machines in around 1986 -87, the data transcription work mechanism
was gradually switched to those new gadgets. The purchase of PC machines also prompted the
authority to shift the software generation work to Data Processing Division, NSSO with the
intention to save some time wasted in the back -and-forth movement of different software
outputs. COBOL (Common Business -Oriented Language ), a high -level programming
language was brought in for development of different software required for data transcription,
data validation and tabulation. This process continued till 1995-96 when a more comprehensive
data transcription software was develop ed by DPD in C language. Other software like data
validation and tabulation, however, continued to run in COBOL platform. The UNIX operating
system was also made operational for faster processing on which most of the software was run
for quick yet reliable output.
Development of in-house software:
Data collection and processing in the NSS underwent another significant transformation in
2002. A new data entry and verification software called DPDSYS was developed internally by
DPD using Visual Basic. This software proved to be user-friendly and highly adaptable, making
it easy to modify for creating data entry applications for any NSS schedule. With necessary
adjustments, DPDSYS was successfully used across multiple survey rounds on diverse topics.
In addition , other supporting software for data validation, multiplier generation, and
intermediate processing —leading up to tabulation —were developed in the C programming
language,

tware for data validation, multiplier generation, and
intermediate processing —leading up to tabulation —were developed in the C programming
language, with built-in flexibility to adapt to new surveys and schedules. A generic tabulation
tool named DOSTAB was also created, enabling the generation of all required NSS tables.
Both DPDSYS and DOSTAB became major milestones for NSS, allowing surveys to be
executed smoothly with a high degree of accuracy and reliability.
Most of these programs were run on the UNIX platform, which allowed quick processing of
large datasets. For state-level data entry, processing, and tabulation of state samples, these tools
were also made available in the DOS environment. Additionally, database tools like Visual
FoxPro were used in DPD as needed.
While the development of these software systems greatly improved the efficiency and accuracy
of survey operations, they still didn’t fully solve the problem of long time-lag. The main reason
for this lag was the presence of several steps and the complex movement of survey schedules
from data collection to finalization. Data collection was still done manually by the Field
Operations Division (FOD) using paper schedules, which were then sent to various Data
Processing Centres (DPCs) for data transcription. To expedite data entry, built-in checks were
kept at a minimum in software , since operators were often working remotely. As a result,
extensive post-entry scrutiny was required, consuming more time to correct both simple errors
and deeper conceptual issues. 110

Era of e-schedule:
In an endeavour to reduce time lag to a certain extent, e -schedule was developed in -house in
NSS 76th round to replace DPDSYS in which necessary validations checks were incorporated
upfront to prevent basic mistakes in the data at the entry stage itself. It was also decided that
paper schedules canvassed in the field will be data entered in that place by investigators
themselves using this application and the digitized data would be sent to DPCs for further
validation. This process somehow cut down the time wasted in dispatching the physical
schedules from field offices to DPCs. It also managed to reduce the processing time since basic
errors could be eliminated at the entry stage itself through those embedded validation checks
in the entry module.
The time consumed in data collection in paper schedule and further its transcription in digital
mode was a common point of contention in different meetings and a feasible solution to address
this problem was felt imperative. It was also emphasized to eliminate most of the
inconsistencies in the data at the collection stage itself so as to reduce the data processing time
required. One more demand was that data validation should be accomplished on real time basis
so that enumerators could be provided feedback on data quality at the earliest. It was decided
that data collection should be initiated through CAPI whic h will have inherent validation
checks to be performed at the time of data collection. In NSS 77 th round Indian Statistical
Institute (ISI) was entrusted with the job of developing such a module leveraging latest
technologies by which field enumerators wil l be able to capture data from the respondent in
digital mode. A browser based offline CAPI was developed by them and field enumerators
would

tors wil l be able to capture data from the respondent in
digital mode. A browser based offline CAPI was developed by them and field enumerators
would go to the field with data collection module uploaded in their tablets. This process indeed
brought in a paradigm shift in data collection methodology by which a considerable period of
data transcription and processing could be saved. But this process was also mired in a few
major bugs for which further improvement in this process was necessitated.
Offline CAPI:
NSS experimented with a web -based CAPI system in 2017, utilizing a solution provided by
the World Bank for the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS). Although it was not an
exhaustive CAPI encompassing both the listing and detailed schedule in totality, yet it was
deployed in the field offices for PLFS data collection. Due to intermittent version change of
World Bank solutions, NSS started facing some serious issues to cope up with those changes
and many problems in data capturing and storage started building up. A s a result, the World
Bank CAPI had to be discontinued after some time and NSS again, albeit for a short period,
used to paper-based data collection.

111

In 78th round of NSS, an in-house offline CAPI software with embedded validation checks was
developed by NSS. Data were collected and stored in tablets and dispatched to DPCs through
email. These data files were further extracted and combined into a bigger data file using another
software. The combined data file was eventually subjected to further validation as per the usual
process of data finalization.
Thus, it is evident that several experiments with different software options were carried out in
the quest of a consistent and viable CAPI which would ensure seamless data collection, storage
and processing through server doing away with all time -consuming steps in between. The 112

objective was to build up a platform in which all necessary processes right from data collection
to data validation could be encapsulated and which could handle several NSS surveys
simultaneously.
Development of Full-fledged CAPI:
It was finally decided in 2019 to outsource the work of developing such an integrated platform
and in this process eSIGMA was conceptualized. The application was developed with the idea
of integrating several modules which were to be customised for each and every survey. Online
server based CAPI for Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS), Household Consumption
Expenditure Survey (HCES) and Annual Survey of Unincorporated Sector Enterprises
(ASUSE) was developed one by one and the surveys ran successfully in the field. Most of the
validation checks were embedded in that CAPI and numerous additional features were
incorporated so that anomaly could be prevented to creep in at the time of data collection.
Survey enumerators were made to give suitable explanation to any apparent aberration in the
data figures at the time of data collection itself and in this process number o f future
correspondences could also be minimized. Data once captured were put through two layers of
online concurrent checking before they were accepted and stored in the server. Any discrepancy
found before acceptance could be communicated to the enumerat or through server so that
immediate action could be taken. Hence, near real time data validation, which used to be a
demand before that period, was made possible to a great extent through eSIGMA application.
Apart from CAPI, one more essential module in eSIGMA was the ‘Dashboard’ module through
which progress of any survey could be monitored at different layers and options. The others

Continuous improvement in CAPI:
At present NSS is gearing up to launch a number of new household and enterprise surveys.
Some household and enterprise surveys are already ongoing in the field. The digital solutions
for these surveys are being developed or refined within the eSIGMA platform, with several
new features being added to enhance functionality. Modern technologies, including Artif icial
Intelligence (AI), are also being integrated into the Computer -Assisted Personal Interviewing
(CAPI) system for use in various surveys. Additionally, other components of eSIGMA are
being upgraded to transform it into a comprehensive and robust platfo rm suitable for any
sample survey.
Efforts are underway to make the CAPI system more agile and user-friendly, ensuring smoother
usage for personnel at all operational levels. For data processing and tabulation, the NSS
currently utilizes a range of softwar e tools —such as Python, R, Visual FoxPro, and C —
depending on the specific needs and ease of use. There are also plans to make the system more
technology-driven and server-oriented, which would help in reducing processing time further
and enable release of survey data and results within shorter period. 113

The Annual Survey of Industries (ASI) has undergone a remarkable technological
transformation in its methods of data collection and processing sin ce its inception in 1960.
Over the decades, the shift from manual paper -based processes to digital platforms has
significantly enhanced operational efficiency, improved data accuracy and reduced the time lag
in disseminating industrial statistics.
For a lo ng period, ASI data were collected through paper schedules by the Field Operations
Division (FOD), NSSO. These filled -in ASI schedules were dispatched to the Industrial
Statistics (IS) Wing, Kolkata, for data processing via post. The information captured i n the
paper schedules was digitized using a data entry module developed in -house in Visual Basic
(VB) with an Oracle database at the IS Wing, Kolkata.
As the filled-in paper schedules had to be dispatched from various field offices to the IS Wing,
Kolkata, through postal services, a considerable amount of time was consumed even before the
data digitization process could commence. Ensuring accuracy during data digitization was also
a significant challenge, which necessitated re -entry of the schedules by diff erent personnel to
identify and rectify any transcription errors in the data. After the re-entry process, the data were
subjected to multiple levels of scrutiny to ensure accuracy and credibility. This rigorous method
was resource-intensive and often delayed the release of results.
e-Schedule Era in ASI (2008-2012):
To reduce the time lag, data collection during ASI 2008–09 was carried out on a pilot basis by
the FOD using an e-schedule developed in MS-Excel format. In ASI 2008–09, approximately
1,486 schedules in MS-Excel format were canvassed and sent

by
the FOD using an e-schedule developed in MS-Excel format. In ASI 2008–09, approximately
1,486 schedules in MS-Excel format were canvassed and sent to the IS Wing for processing.
In ASI 2009–10, an e-schedule in MS-Access format was developed in-house aiming to cover
10,000 schedules out of the total 61,080 schedules as part of an experimental initiative .
Subsequently, ASI 2010–11 and ASI 2011–12 data were collected through the e -schedule in
MS-Access format for all the selected units in the survey. In e -schedule built -in validation
checks were incorporated to prevent basic errors at the data entry stage itself. The filled-in e-
schedules were sent to the IS Wing, Kolkata, through email. Data continued to be processed
using in-house tools like Visual FoxPro and Oracle, while final outputs were exported in Excel
for dissemination.
This system also helped to reduce the overall processing time, as basic errors could be
eliminated at the entry stage itself through the embedded validation checks in the entry module.

114

Web Portal Era in ASI (2012 Onwards):
Starting from ASI 2012–13, a major leap occurred with the launch of a dedicated web portal.
This portal enabled direct data entry with embedded validation at the source itself, ensuring
real-time error detection, improved accuracy, and reduced field -to-desk time. The portal
provides 24×7 secure access, eliminatin g physical movement of schedules. It also facilitates
faster processing, seamless integration with databases, dynamic frame updation, automated
sample selection, real-time monitoring of data collection progress, and dissemination of ASI
data. From ASI 2018-19 onwards, ASI was also integrated into the eSIGMA platform marking
a significant leap in to the adoption of evolving technologies over the decades which reflects
its commitment to delivering high-quality data in a transparent, timely, and efficient manner.

115

Conclusion:
Over the decades, the National Sample Survey (NSS) has undergone a remarkable
transformation in its approach to data collection and processing. In its early decades, data
collection was entirely manual, involving paper schedules and card -punch-based digitization.
Thereafter, software like DPDSYS for data transcription and DOSTAB as generic tabulation
tool were developed in -house. Subsequently, data collection mode shifted from PAPI to
Computer-Assisted Personal Interviewing (CAPI). Development of Web -portal for ASI and
CAPI for other NSS surveys under the integrated digital platform eSIGMA, enabled real-time
validation, minimizing errors at the point of data collection, and reducing reliance on manual
intervention.
With ongoing advancements, including the i ntegration of some features of Artificial
Intelligence and enhanced dashboard monitoring, NSS is poised to become a fully modern,
tech-enabled survey system. These innovations not only streamline operations but also ensure
high quality, credible data—critical for informed decision-making and evidence-based policy
planning. As NSS continues to evolve, its focus remains firmly on building a robust, adaptable,
and future -ready data ecosystem capable of supporting the nation ’s socio -economic
development goal.

2 1. Introduction Consumer Price Indices (CPIs) measure changes over time in the general level of prices of goods
and services that households acquire (use or pay for) for the purpose of consumption (Graf B,
2020). CPI is a macroeconomic indicator, universally in use, as a measure of inflation, and as a
tool for, inflation targeting, monitoring price stability, and as deflators in the national accounts, by
governments and central banks. The indicator is often included in legislations as well in service
contracts as the appropriate measure for accounting of inflation and adjusting bill payments related
to wages, rents, interest, social security, pensions, etc. Therefore, CPI has a substantial and wide-
ranging financial implications for governments, businesses, as well as households.

For measuring the aggregate price changes, a sample variety of items are selected from sample
outlets that represent the goods and services consumed by the households. The usual method of
calculation is to take an average of the period -to-period price changes for the different products,
and weights being the average amounts that households spend on them. CPIs are official statistics
that are usually produced by NSOs, ministries of labour, or central banks. They are published as
quickly as possible, generally within two-three weeks after the reference period.
The prices are collected from shops or other retail outlets. The price collectors are given detailed
item descr iptions defining each item variety, its specifications and location. The detailed
specifications are included on the price collection template each period and serve as a prompt to
help ensure that the same varieties are being priced. As any lack of clarity in the specifications
may lead to errors , d etailed checklists o f variety descriptions are used. In addition, adequate
attention is paid to include all details for identification of the variety and outlet on a subsequent
visit. For example , along with details of the outlet location, all pertinent price-determining
characteristics are included, to ensure identification of changes in quality have occurred.
For compilation of the CPI, generally, the methodology adopted is illustrated here:
(a) Firstly, the price indices are computed for elementary aggregates, known as price relatives,
(ratios of current prices over base prices each item -wise). The elementary aggregate can
include stratification by item variety, region and by shop type or market.

3 (b) The elementary item indices are aggregated using Geometric Mean (GM) of the Price
Relatives of Current Prices with respect to Base Prices of different markets in consonance with
the international practice.

price indices. Explicit expenditure weights are available at this level of aggregation. Then
using consumption expenditure as weights, associated with each level, the elementary price
indices are averaged (aggregated) to obtain higher level indices. This is done here with the

observe a price in the current period, may have obtained information (for example, from the

unknown, time in the future (Graf B, 2020).

Simply said, missing data are observations that were meant to be measured but were not because
of their inevitable nature. Missing observations often result in incomplete data sets, a problem that
almost every research study faces. It is often said that one should be surprised if no data is missing.
However, the problem is not taken as serious by investigators or researchers because they do not
understand the implications of the missing data on the final result. However, a number of
researchers have been working in this area and have been proposing different analytical methods
to handle this problem. The literature available on the subject has been growing and reflects the
fact that the last word, on incomplete data issues, is yet to be pronounced.

While dealing with missing values it is often assumed that a small number of rows with missing
entries in the data matrix (Rencher, 2002), does not constitute a serious problem. Each row that
has a missing value is simply discarded. However, with this procedure, if the small portion of
missing data is widely distributed, it would lead to a substantial loss of data. For example, in a
large data set with sample size, n = 550 and variable size, p= 85, if only about 1.5% of the 550 ×
85 = 46,750 measurements were missing, but nearly half of the observation vectors (rows of Y)
turned out to be incomplete , as it depends on the spread of the missing values across differen t
rows. The distribution of missing values in a data set is an important consideration. Randomly
missing variable values scattered throughout a data matrix are assumed to be less serious than a
pattern of missing values that depends to some extent on the values of the missing variables.

6 The most widely used missing data classification system that evolved in literature was first
introduced by Rubin (1976), who specified three distinct missing data types:
(1) Missing Completely at Random (MCAR),
(2) Missing at Random (MAR) and
(3) Missing Not at Random (MNAR). The missing data types introduced by Rubin (1976), also relate to the extent of bias that the missing
data may exert on the statistical analyses. I n the spectrum of MCAR to MNAR, the impact of
MCAR on bias is likely to be negligible, whereas with MNAR the impact is likely to be greatest. All of the causes for missing data were further classified into four classes (also called mechanisms),
based on the relationship be tween the missing data mechanism and the missing and observed
values (Martin, 2001; Little & Rubin, 2002; Schafer & Graham, 2002; Enders, 2013). It is
important to understand the four classes as the solutions to the problems caused by missing data
are different for the four classes. i. The MCAR assumption being the most stringent of the missing data mechanisms, that can
be checked using Little’s multivariate test for MCAR (Little, 1988), but unfortunately most
missing data are not MCAR.

mechanism is related to the missing values. For example, in a survey people do not want to
respond to something very personal about themselves or something that is unpopular. In an
income-survey, i t is less likely that higher income individuals reveal income related
information, as compared to lower income individuals, which makes missing data on income
non-ignorable. Here the value of income determines whether it is observed or missing . At
the end of the survey, for income related information, if the proportion of observed data is
more among low and moderate -income individuals in the sample, than the higher -income
individuals, the estimate of mean income would be lower than the actual p opulation mean.
Therefore, complete case analysis, that is analysis based on only fully observed cases, can
give highly biased results for NI missing data.

income survey, an example for CD missing data could be that missing income data are not

may be possible that people with higher education, have not responded to the income related
information as compared to individuals with less education. In short MCAR implies that ‘ Missing mechanism’ does not depend on the observed or missing

Various techniques exist as a solution to missing data, ranging from data deletion to methods that
replace each missing value with an imputed value employing simple statistical analyses methods
to techniques based on artificial intelligence. Imputation is the most common solution to handle

8 missing data, where the missing values are estimated and filled in. An important problem of
imputation is to preserve the statistical distribution of the data set. This is a complex problem,
especially for high -dimensional data. In this paper the d escription of the missing data analyses
methods is restricted to the two methods, OMI and MI, adopted and compared here. 4.3 Imputation Algorithms
Imputation methods may be broadly classified into two categories: random and deterministic
(Ming-xiu & Salvucci, 2001). The deterministic imputation approach imputes one and only one
possible value to replace each missing value. Once, the imputation scheme is set up, the imputation
result is unique. On the other hand, a random imputation method draws imputation value s
randomly either from the observed data or from the predicted distribution. Multiple sets of
imputations can be created to capture the uncertainty between imputations via any random
imputation method. Generally, a random imputation method adds more variability to the statistics
computed from an imputed data set than a deterministic imputation method. 4.3.1 Overall Mean Imputation
In this method, for a temporarily missing price of an item, the current month price is
imputed/derived by multiplying price of the same item in the previous month with average price
relative of current month prices to last month prices from rest of markets of the same item where
both current and previous month prices are available. The imputation is generally done within
town in case of Urban-Index and within state in case of Rural-Index.
